Trieste-style Sauerkraut

Trieste-style sauerkraut stewed with onion, flour, lard, and caraway.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

2 1/4 lb sauerkraut
1 onion, finely chopped
2 tbsp flour
2 tbsp lard
2 cups plus 2 tbsp water
1 tsp caraway seeds
3/4 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper

Preparation

1. Put the sauerkraut in a saucepan.

2. Add the water, or enough to come almost level with the sauerkraut.

3. Bring to a gentle boil.

4. Cook for about 30 minutes.

5. Meanwhile, melt the lard in a second saucepan.

6. Add the onion.

7. Cook for 5 minutes.

8. Add the flour.

9. Stir for 2–3 minutes, until lightly nut-brown.

10. Add the sauerkraut and all of its cooking water to the onion mixture.

11. Add the salt, pepper, and caraway.

12. Cover.

13. Cook over very low heat for 30–40 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes.

14. Uncover during the final minutes and let the liquid evaporate completely.

Service

Serve very hot with boiled meats or sausages.

Chef's note

Toasting the flour in the lard naturally binds the sauerkraut and thickens its cooking liquid during the second stage.

Cabbage stewed with tomato, garlic, butter, olive oil, and lemon zest, finished with Grana.

Preparation

1. Remove the toughest outer cabbage leaves.

Brovada

Friulian fermented turnips slowly cooked with lard, onion, herbs, and pork broth.

Yield: 6 servings

Ingredients

about 2 2/3 lb fermented shredded brovada
about 3/4 cup finely chopped lard
2 onions, finely chopped
2 garlic cloves, minced
1/4 cup finely chopped fresh parsley
6 sage leaves
4 1/4 cups hot pork broth
3/4 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper

Preparation

1. Taste the brovada.

2. If excessively sour, rinse it briefly in cool water and squeeze dry.

3. Put the lard in an earthenware pot or heavy saucepan.

4. Add the onions.

5. Cook over low heat for 8 minutes.

6. Add the garlic, parsley, and sage.

7. Cook for 1 minute.

8. Add the brovada.

9. Pour in 2 cups plus 2 tablespoons broth.

10. Cover partially.

11. Cook over very low heat for 2–3 hours.

12. Stir every 20 minutes.

13. Add more broth in 1/2-cup portions whenever the pan becomes dry.

14. Continue until the brovada turns chestnut-brown and becomes very tender.

15. Adjust the salt and pepper only at the end.

Service

Serve very hot with musetto, cotechino, or boiled pork.

Chef's note

The long cooking rounds out the acidity of the fermented turnips. Add broth gradually instead of flooding the pot.

Soft Frico

Friulian soft frico made with potatoes, onion, and Montasio, browned on both sides.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

1 1/3 lb potatoes
about 3 cups diced Montasio in mixed ages
1 small white or yellow onion, thinly sliced
2 tbsp oil
1 cup water, divided
3/4 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a nonstick skillet.

2. Add the onion.

3. Add 1/4 cup water.

4. Cook gently for 5–6 minutes.

5. Peel the potatoes and slice them very thin.

6. Add them to the onion.

7. Add 1/2 cup water.

8. Cover partially.

9. Cook slowly for about 40 minutes, stirring gently and adding the remaining water only if needed.

10. Coarsely mash some of the potatoes with a spoon.

11. Add the Montasio.

12. Stir until completely melted.

13. Add the salt.

14. Press the mixture into an even cake in the skillet.

15. Cook without stirring until the bottom is golden.

16. Turn with the help of a plate.

17. Cook the second side until crisp and browned.

Service

Rest for 5 minutes and cut into wedges.

Chef's note

The center should remain soft and stretchy while only the outer surfaces become crisp.

Crispy Frico

Thin crisp Friulian wafers made from aged Montasio cheese.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

about 3 cups finely grated 16–18-month Montasio
1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil

Preparation

1. Finely grate the Montasio.

2. Lightly grease a nonstick skillet about 6 inches wide with a very small amount of the olive oil.

4. Scatter about one-quarter of the cheese in a thin even layer.

5. Cook until melted and golden underneath, about 2–3 minutes.

7. Cook the second side for 1–2 minutes.

8. Transfer to parchment or a wire rack.

9. Repeat with the remaining cheese.

Service

Serve flat as a crisp wafer or shape while still hot over an inverted bowl to make a basket.

Chef's note

Crispy frico should be very thin. A thick layer retains more fat and stays soft in the center.

4 heads late-season Treviso radicchio
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil

Perugia-style cardoons boiled, fried, layered with meat ragù and Parmigiano, and baked until golden.

Vitello Tonnato

Piedmont veal round marinated in white wine, gently cooked, chilled, and served with tuna, anchovy, egg, and caper sauce.

Yield: 8 servings

Ingredients

For the veal
2 1/4 lb veal eye round
1 1/4 cups dry white wine
1 celery stalk, cut into pieces
2 bay leaves
6 sage leaves
3 whole cloves
2 1/8 qt water, approximately, for cooking
1 2/3 tsp fine salt

For the tuna sauce
about 2 cups drained oil-packed tuna
6 oil-packed anchovy fillets
3 hard-boiled egg yolks
1 heaping tbsp pickled capers, plus 1 tbsp for garnish
juice of 1 lemon
1/2 cup extra-virgin olive oil
1 tbsp white-wine vinegar
1 cup veal cooking broth, approximately
6 pickled gherkins for serving

Preparation

1. Trim any outer membrane from the veal.

2. Put the meat in a bowl.

3. Pour in the white wine.

4. Add the celery, bay leaves, sage, and cloves.

5. Cover and marinate in the refrigerator for at least 12 hours.

6. Transfer the veal to a saucepan.

7. Strain the marinade and pour it over the meat.

8. Add enough water to cover the veal generously.

9. Add the salt.

10. Bring to a boil.

11. Reduce the heat and cook for about 1 hour.

12. Drain the meat, reserving at least 1 cup cooking broth.

13. Cool for 2 hours.

14. Refrigerate for 1 hour so it becomes firm enough to slice thinly.

15. Blend the tuna, yolks, anchovies, capers, lemon juice, olive oil, and vinegar.

16. Gradually add cooking broth until the sauce is smooth and velvety.

17. Slice the veal very thinly.

Service

Arrange the slices on plates, cover generously with tuna sauce, and finish with capers and gherkins.

Chef's note

Chilling the meat completely before slicing produces thin, even slices without tearing the veal.
